method: Loudness level in phons and loudness in sones describe the same percept on two scales. By definition the phon figure of a sound is the sound pressure level of a 1 kHz pure tone that listeners judge equally loud, so at 1 kHz the phon number and the dB SPL number are the same. One sone is the loudness of a 1 kHz tone at 40 dB SPL, and loudness doubles for every 10 phon, which is Stevens' power law with an exponent near 0.3 written in its doubling form: sone = 2^((phon - 40) / 10) and phon = 40 + 10 x log2(sone). The page accepts either quantity with a reference level in phons, and reports the matching figure, the level at 1 kHz in dB SPL, the ratio to the reference as a multiple of its sone value with the doublings behind it, the level difference in phon and dB, and the levels that would double or halve the loudness. Values are limited to 0 to 140 phon, the 0.0625 to 1024 sone the scale covers; a value outside that range, a reference outside it, an unknown unit, a word instead of a number, a loudness of zero or less, or a length reading with no digits is refused with the reason. Below 40 phon the straight power law overstates quietness because the equal-loudness contours flatten near the threshold of hearing, so results under 40 phon are marked indicative; the law describes single tones and narrowband signals, and a broadband signal needs a critical-band loudness model such as the one in ISO 532 rather than a single sone value. Everything is computed in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.
